passage:
Monday. Parul and Harish were playing carrom on the veranda when Harish said her striker had touched the line, so she must give up the queen. "It did not touch," said Parul. "It did," said Harish. Both folded their arms and the game stopped.

Wednesday. The same fight started again. This time Parul said, "Here is what I saw. Now you tell me what you saw." Harish told her. Neither changed their mind, so Parul suggested asking Harish's cousin to watch.

Saturday. The cousin sat between them and called every close shot the same way for both. They agreed on a new rule: a striker on the line loses the turn. The game lasted all afternoon.

qa.q: Where were Parul and Harish playing carrom?
qa.a: They were playing on the veranda.

qa.q: Why did Parul say, "Now you tell me what you saw"?
qa.a: She wanted to hear Harish's side and settle the argument fairly, not just repeat her own view, even though both still felt sure they were right.

qa.q: What could the two of them do if the cousin is not around next time?
qa.a: They could write the line rule down together before starting, or ask another fair person to watch the close shots.

qa.q: How might Harish see Parul's idea of asking Harish's cousin?
qa.a: Harish may have felt relieved that someone neutral could decide, though Harish might also have worried the cousin would rule against Harish.

grounding: Two friends both claim to be right in a carrom dispute; one states her view, hears the other and they bring in a fair referee and agree a rule.

passage: The mango orchard behind the tea stall was where Ritu and Zubin played marbles after school. Today Zubin's marble stopped at the edge of the circle and he swore it was still inside. Ritu was sure it had crossed the line. She looked at his hopeful face, at the shadows growing long, and at the game they had only half finished. "Fine, it's inside," she said, and flicked her next marble. Zubin grinned and told her to take an extra shot. In her head she kept it small: one marble was not worth an evening spent sulking on separate walls. When the tea stall owner called out that it was getting dark, they walked home together, already arguing about tomorrow's game.

qa.q: Where did Ritu and Zubin play marbles?
qa.a: They played in the mango orchard behind the tea stall.

qa.q: Why did Ritu say, "Fine, it's inside"?
qa.a: She cared more about finishing the game with her friend than about one marble, so she let the small point go.

qa.q: What could Ritu try if Zubin kept claiming every close call?
qa.a: She could give in on small ones but suggest they mark a clear line or pick a fair judge, so the game stays fair for both of them.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel about what Ritu did?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and grateful, and offering her an extra shot suggests he noticed she had given something up. 😊

grounding: Ritu gives in on a small marbles point to keep the game and friendship going, valuing the friend above winning.

passage: My name is Nirmala. Last term I lost the chess club game to Tenzin, and I was so angry that I called him a cheat and a show-off in front of everyone. I said the same things at lunch, and I stopped saying hello. I thought that if Tenzin was my enemy, losing would hurt less. It did not. Then Tenzin left a note on my desk: "Want a rematch on Friday? I will show you the opening I practise." I felt silly. The game was one thing, and Tenzin was another. On Friday we played again. I lost by a little, but for the first time I laughed.

qa.q: What did Nirmala call Tenzin after losing the chess game?
qa.a: Nirmala called him a cheat and a show-off in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala think of Tenzin as an enemy?
qa.a: Nirmala thought that if Tenzin was an enemy, losing would hurt less, so the taunts came from hurt pride, though the plan did not work.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do the next time Nirmala loses a game?
qa.a: Nirmala could notice the sting, say well played or ask about the winning idea, and keep the game separate from the person.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt when Nirmala taunted him?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and confused because he had only played chess, but his note suggests he still wanted to be friends. 🙂

grounding: Nirmala treats the winner as an enemy and taunts, then learns to separate the game from the person.

passage: When the teacher read out "First prize: Soo-ah," the whole class in Lisbon clapped, and Paulo clapped too. His hands were moving, but his stomach felt tight. Soo-ah was his best friend. She had spent three weekends on her drawing of a lighthouse. He was proud of her, and he also wished his own painting of a bus had been picked. After class he walked up to her. "Your lighthouse was really good," he said, and he meant it. That night he took out a fresh sheet and began drawing buses again, this time practising windows and shadows, the way Soo-ah had practised waves.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah draw for the prize?
qa.a: She drew a lighthouse.

qa.q: What was Paulo feeling while he clapped?
qa.a: He felt proud of his best friend and jealous at the same time; the tight stomach shows the sting even while his hands clapped. 🤔

qa.q: How did Paulo turn the sting into something useful?
qa.a: He congratulated Soo-ah honestly and then practised his own drawing, working on windows and shadows.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah see Paulo's words after class?
qa.a: She probably felt happy that her best friend was glad for her, and she may not have known about the sting he felt.

grounding: Paulo feels jealousy and pride together about a best friend's prize, congratulates her and uses it to practise more.

passage: Swati won the recitation prize, and Neelam did not clap. All through the noisy bus ride home from the school trip, she whispered to the girls nearby that the judge was Swati's neighbour and that Swati's mother had written the poem. She did not know if either was true. By the time the bus stopped, the whispers had travelled to the back seat. Next morning three classmates looked at Swati strangely, and Swati sat alone. Neelam expected to feel better. Instead she could not focus on her spelling test, and her stomach hurt each time she remembered what she had said. By Friday Swati's friends had told her it was not true and the talk faded, but Neelam was still carrying the knot.

qa.q: Where did Neelam whisper the rumour?
qa.a: She whispered it during the noisy bus ride home from the school trip.

qa.q: What did Neelam believe about Swati's win, and how sure was she?
qa.a: She believed the win was unfair, but she did not know if her claims were true, so the belief came more from resentment than from facts.

qa.q: What could Neelam do to loosen the knot she was carrying?
qa.a: She could tell the girls she was not sure what she had said was true, and put that energy into practising her own recitation.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt when classmates looked at her strangely?
qa.a: Swati was probably hurt and confused after only winning a prize, and sitting alone suggests the whispers reached Swati.

grounding: Neelam believes the prize was unfair, gossips, and finds the resentment hurts her more than it hurts the winner.

passage: Harsha won the running race at the village school's sports day, and Uday stood at the rope with his mouth open. He had never seen anyone start so fast. The next morning Uday watched Harsha jogging along the canal bank before school. At recess he asked, "What do you do before a race? How do you start so quickly?" Harsha showed him how to crouch low and push off the back foot, and said he ran along the canal every morning, even in the cold. Uday nodded and repeated the steps under his breath. The next day, at first light, Uday was on the canal bank, trying the crouch start again and again while Harsha called out corrections.

qa.q: Where did Harsha run every morning?
qa.a: He ran along the canal every morning, even in the cold.

qa.q: What did Uday feel about Harsha's win, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He admired Harsha; his open mouth, his questions and his early start the next day show he wanted to learn how it was done. 😊

qa.q: What small step would help Uday keep improving?
qa.a: He could keep the morning practice, notice what changes each week and ask Harsha for feedback on his start.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel when Uday asks for tips?
qa.a: He probably felt pleased and a little proud that his effort was noticed, and glad to have company on the canal bank.

grounding: Uday studies how the race winner practised and asks for tips, turning admiration into a role model.

passage: Ms Ingrid handed back the stories at school in Bergen. On Astrid's page she had written: the ending is rushed. Astrid frowned, then raised her hand. "Do you mean I should show what the fox feels before he leaves?" Ms Ingrid nodded. "Yes, give the reader one more moment." At home Astrid rewrote the last paragraph, adding the fox sitting by the river, unsure whether to go. She wanted to keep her title, though, which Ms Ingrid had called plain. The next day she said, "I tried your idea for the ending. I'd like to keep my title, because it sounds like the story to me." Ms Ingrid smiled and said that was a fair reason.

qa.q: What did Ms Ingrid write on Astrid's page?
qa.a: She wrote that the ending is rushed.

qa.q: Why did Astrid ask about the fox's feelings?
qa.a: She wanted to understand the feedback exactly so she could use it, which shows she took it as guidance and not as blame.

qa.q: Why was it reasonable for Astrid to keep her title?
qa.a: She applied the advice about the ending and also gave a clear, polite reason for her own choice, so disagreeing was not the same as ignoring the teacher.

qa.q: How might Ms Ingrid feel about Astrid's reply?
qa.a: She was probably pleased, since Astrid used the advice and also thought for herself, and she accepted the reason with a smile.

grounding: A pupil treats feedback as guidance, asks a follow-up, applies it, and respectfully disagrees on one point.

passage: Note from Vasudha, class teacher. Parul has stopped handing in her maths corrections since I marked her fraction test with "show your steps." She told the girl beside her, "The teacher doesn't like me, so why bother." Her notebook is neat but half empty, and she keeps her eyes on the desk when I pass. On Thursday I sat with her at recess and told her the comment was about the steps, not about her, and pointed to two questions she had got fully right. She was quiet, then asked if I could show one step again. I did. On Friday she handed in three corrected sums. This week I will keep my comments short and specific, and start with what went well.

qa.q: What did Vasudha write on Parul's fraction test?
qa.a: Vasudha wrote "show your steps."

qa.q: What did Parul believe about her teacher, and what did she do because of it?
qa.a: She believed the teacher does not like her, so she stopped handing in corrections and kept her eyes on the desk.

qa.q: How could Vasudha keep Parul's progress alive?
qa.a: By keeping comments short and specific, making clear they are about the work and not about Parul, and showing a step again when she asks.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt when the test came back with that comment?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and discouraged, hearing it as a judgement of her, so she pulled back from the work.

grounding: A pupil takes marking as dislike and stops trying; the teacher separates the feedback from the person and progress resumes.

passage: Evening note from Himani. Today my daughter Pallavi sat with my mother while Nani explained why the pickle jar must be dried in the sun before it is closed. Pallavi did not interrupt once. She nodded and watched Nani's hands. Then she asked, quite gently, "Nani, why does the jar have to be dry?" Nani said water lets mould grow, and that her own mother had taught her, and that she learned it the hard way when one jar spoiled. Pallavi said, "So that is why. Can I turn the jars with you tomorrow?" I stayed out of it. I noticed I was proud, and that Nani looked happy to be asked.

qa.q: What did Nani say must be done to the pickle jar before it is closed?
qa.a: She said it must be dried in the sun.

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel toward Nani as she listened, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She listened without interrupting and then gently asked why, and she asked to help the next day, which shows respect and curiosity together.

qa.q: How could Himani support this kind of listening at home?
qa.a: Himani could keep stepping back and invite Nani to share more of what Nani has learned, while letting Pallavi ask questions.

qa.q: What might Nani have felt when Pallavi asked why?
qa.a: She probably felt valued, since the question showed Pallavi cared about the experience behind the advice, and Himani noticed Nani looked happy.

grounding: A child listens to a grandmother without interrupting and still politely asks why.

passage: Note from Binita, after-school club. At pick-up on Tuesday, Divyansh's father reminded him for the third time to pack his bag the night before. Divyansh rolled his eyes and stared at the wall with his arms crossed. On Wednesday I asked him quietly what that was like. He said, "It's like he thinks I can't remember anything." We practised a sentence he could say instead of sulking or shouting. On Thursday his father began the same reminder and Divyansh answered, "I heard you, Papa. Let me try my way this week." His father paused, then said all right. I will check in with both of them next week.

qa.q: How many times had Divyansh's father reminded him about the bag at pick-up?
qa.a: He reminded him for the third time.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he rolled his eyes?
qa.a: He felt lectured and underestimated; he said it was like his father thinks he can't remember anything.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that worked better than sulking or shouting?
qa.a: He said, "I heard you, Papa. Let me try my way this week," which acknowledged his father and asked for room.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's father see the reminders?
qa.a: He probably meant them as care and worry about a forgotten bag, so hearing that Divyansh had heard him helped him step back.

grounding: A child feels lectured by a parent, rolls eyes, then learns to say I heard you and asks to try their own way.
